blocks.h: 1. What goal-based standards are, and why they exist

blocks.p: A prescriptive rule tells a designer what to build. A goal-based standard states what the ship must achieve and leaves the detailed rules to be written beneath it, then verifies that those rules deliver the goal. The International Goal-based Ship Construction Standards for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers were adopted by resolution MSC.287(87) on 20 May 2010. They are given force through SOLAS regulation II-1/3-10, adopted by resolution MSC.290(87) and, with the definition at II-1/2.28, in force from 1 January 2012. They apply to bulk carriers and oil tankers of 150 m in length and above for which the building contract is placed on or after 1 July 2016.

The reason for the change of approach is that prescriptive scantling rules had grown from experience of past failures, differed between societies, and gave the Organization no way of saying what level of safety they were actually delivering. GBS fixes the required outcome at IMO level and makes the rule-writer demonstrate conformity with it.

blocks.h: 2. The tier structure - and how many tiers the instrument actually contains

blocks.p: This is the discrimination the question rewards, and it is where most published summaries go wrong. Section 1.5 of MSC.287(87) records that the Committee agreed to use a five-tier system:

ul: Tier I - Goals
Tier II - Functional requirements
Tier III - Verification of conformity
Tier IV - Rules and regulations for ship design and construction
Tier V - Industry practices and standards

blocks.p: But section 3, STRUCTURE, states that "These Standards consist of the following three tiers: Tier I, Tier II, Tier III." The framework is five tiers; the instrument itself contains three. Tiers IV and V are the class and national rules and the industry practice that sit beneath the Standards and are measured against them - they are not part of the Standards. Say both halves of that and the point is made.

blocks.h: 3. Tier I and Tier II - the goal and the functional requirements

blocks.p: Tier I is a single goal: ships shall be designed and constructed for a specified design life to be safe and environmentally friendly when properly operated and maintained under the specified operating and environmental conditions, in intact and specified damage conditions, throughout their life. Its sub-goals require adequate strength, integrity and stability; construction from materials permitting environmentally acceptable recycling; safe access, escape, inspection and maintenance; specified operating and environmental conditions; and a specified design life.
Tier II contains fifteen functional requirements, and they fall into four lifecycle groups, which is the natural skeleton for this part of the answer:

ul: Design - design life (not less than 25 years); environmental conditions (North Atlantic); structural strength; fatigue life; residual strength; protection against corrosion, including coating life and corrosion addition; structural redundancy; watertight and weathertight integrity; human element considerations; design transparency.
Construction - construction quality procedures; survey during construction.
In-service considerations - survey and maintenance; structural accessibility.
Recycling considerations - recycling.

blocks.h: 4. Why this enhances safety and environmental protection

blocks.p: Safety is raised because the goal is expressed over the whole life rather than at delivery: a minimum design life of 25 years, North Atlantic environmental conditions as the design basis, explicit fatigue and residual-strength requirements, and structural redundancy so that a single failure is not immediately catastrophic. Requiring structural accessibility and design transparency means the ship can actually be inspected and maintained, and that the assumptions behind the scantlings survive the designer.

Environmental protection is not an afterthought bolted on to a safety instrument. It is written into the Tier I goal itself - the ship must be environmentally friendly, must be built of materials that allow environmentally acceptable recycling, and carries a Tier II functional requirement for recycling. Coating life and corrosion addition also matter environmentally, because the loss of a tanker or bulk carrier through corrosion-driven structural failure is a pollution event before it is anything else.

Tier III is the verification layer. Under section 6.1, the rules of an organization recognized by an Administration in accordance with SOLAS regulation XI-1/1, or the national rules of an Administration, shall be verified as conforming to the goals and functional requirements. Verification is done at IMO, not by the rule-writer certifying itself: an International GBS Audit Team established by the Secretary-General evaluates the submission and reports to the Maritime Safety Committee for approval.

The guidelines used are the current revision, not the original. Conformity is now assessed against the Revised guidelines for verification of conformity with goal-based ship construction standards, resolution MSC.454(100). Citing the original MSC.296(87) as the operative guideline is a currency error.

ul: IMO / MSC - owns Tiers I to III, appoints the audit teams and approves the verification outcome.
The Administration - recognizes organizations under SOLAS XI-1/1, may submit its own national rules for verification, and remains responsible for the flag State duty however much it delegates.

Classification societies as recognized organizations - write the Tier IV rules, submit them for GBS verification, and carry out survey during construction under Tier II. Collectively, through IACS, they produced the Common Structural Rules for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers as the harmonised Tier IV instrument.
Ship designers - deliver the design life, the human element considerations and the design transparency the Standards require.
Shipbuilders - work to the construction quality procedures, accept survey during construction, and compile the Ship Construction File.
Shipowners and operators - keep the ship to the assumptions the design was built on, and maintain and update the Ship Construction File through the ship's life.

blocks.p: The ship-level output of the whole scheme is the Ship Construction File, required by SOLAS regulation II-1/3-10.2.1, with the content addressed by MSC.1/Circ.1343. It is provided at delivery, kept on board and/or ashore, and updated through the ship's life so that the information needed for safe operation, maintenance, survey, repair and emergency response stays available. It is the practical answer to design transparency: without it, the reasoning behind the structure is lost the moment the yard closes the file.

Two limbs of eight marks each, and they ask different things. Limb (a) is concept plus significance - so it needs the tier structure, the goal and functional requirements, and then a deliberate paragraph that answers why this makes ships safer and cleaner. Limb (b) is process plus people, and the examiner has named three of the stakeholders for you. A very common failure is to write one long essay on what GBS are and never reach the verification process or the stakeholder roles, forfeiting half the question. Sections 1 to 4 are limb (a); sections 5 to 7 are limb (b).

blocks.h: The tier count is the discriminator

blocks.p: Almost every summary of GBS states a single number of tiers, and they disagree with one another. The instrument settles it, and it says two things that are both true: the Committee agreed a five-tier system (section 1.5), and the Standards themselves consist of three tiers (section 3). An automated summary of this very resolution asserted a "four-tier hierarchical framework", which is neither. If you write "five tiers, of which the Standards contain the first three, with class and national rules at Tier IV and industry practice at Tier V", you have said something no summary-reader can say, and it is correct.

blocks.h: Goal-based is not the same as non-prescriptive

blocks.p: GBS does not abolish prescriptive rules - it subordinates them. Tier IV is still a thick book of scantling rules, and a ship is still built to it. What changed is that the rule book must now be demonstrated, at IMO, to deliver a goal that IMO wrote. Candidates who describe GBS as "performance-based instead of prescriptive rules" have half the idea; the sharper statement is that GBS puts a verified goal above the prescriptive rules.

ul: Giving a single tier count without saying whether it is the framework or the instrument.
Citing MSC.296(87) as the verification guideline. It has been superseded; the operative revision is MSC.454(100).
Saying GBS applies to all ships. It applies to bulk carriers and oil tankers of 150 m and above, by building-contract date.
Confusing the adopting resolutions: MSC.287(87) adopts the Standards, MSC.290(87) adopts the SOLAS regulation that makes them mandatory.
Treating GBS as purely structural. The Tier I goal expressly requires the ship to be environmentally friendly and recyclable.
Forgetting the Ship Construction File, which is the only part of GBS a serving engineer actually handles.

blocks.p:
"Who verifies that a classification society's rules meet the goals?" Not the society, and not the flag State alone - an International GBS Audit Team established by the IMO Secretary-General, reporting to the MSC for approval. The society cannot self-certify conformity.

"Is a ship built to class rules automatically GBS-compliant?" Only if those rules have been verified as conforming and the ship falls within the application. The chain is: verified Tier IV rules, applied to a ship of the right type, size and contract date, with a Ship Construction File delivered.

"What is the design life?" Not less than 25 years, with North Atlantic environmental conditions as the design basis. These two numbers are the ones most often asked and most often missed.

ul: Which resolution adopted the Standards, and which made them mandatory? MSC.287(87) and MSC.290(87).
Which SOLAS regulation carries them? II-1/3-10, with the definition at II-1/2.28, in force 1 January 2012.
Name the four lifecycle groups of the Tier II functional requirements. Design, construction, in-service considerations, recycling.
What is the Ship Construction File and where is it kept? SOLAS II-1/3-10.2.1; on board and/or ashore, updated through the ship's life.
Which regulation governs recognition of the organization whose rules are verified? SOLAS XI-1/1.
Name the harmonised Tier IV instrument. The IACS Common Structural Rules for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers.

questions.understand_first: Regulation traditionally told a builder what to do: this plate thickness, that scantling. The trouble with a prescriptive rule is that it freezes yesterday's design and gives a designer no credit for a better idea. Goal-based standards invert that. The regulator states the outcome the ship must achieve, and for how long she must go on achieving it; somebody else decides how. That produces a layered structure - at the top a plain statement of what a safe ship is, beneath it the things she must functionally be able to do in order to be that, and beneath that the detailed rules a classification society writes and must then prove actually deliver the goal above them. That proof step is the real novelty: class rules are no longer simply accepted, they are audited upward against the goal. Everything else in the question - who does what, and the file handed over at delivery - follows from the fact that the goal and the rule are now written by different people.

blocks.p: Port State control is the inspection of foreign ships in national ports to verify that the condition of the ship and its equipment, and the competence and manning of the crew, comply with the requirements of international conventions, and that the ship is operated in accordance with them. It is a safety net, not the primary line of defence: the primary duty to ensure compliance rests with the flag State, and port State control exists because some flag States do not discharge it effectively. It does not transfer that duty, and it does not certify a ship as fit.

It is exercised in practice through regional memoranda of understanding, which pool inspection data, target ships by risk profile and publish detention records. India is a member of the Indian Ocean Memorandum of Understanding.

The power is not free-standing: it is conferred by the conventions themselves, and the current procedures are set out in resolution A.1206(34), Procedures for Port State Control, 2025, adopted 3 December 2025. Section 1.4 lists the provisions relied on:

ul: SOLAS 1974 - regulations I/19, IX/6.2, XI-1/4 and XI-2/9, as modified by the 1988 SOLAS Protocol;
Load Lines 1966 - article 21, as modified by the 1988 LL Protocol;
MARPOL - articles 5 and 6, and regulation 11 of Annex I, regulation 16.9 of Annex II, regulation 9 of Annex III, regulation 14 of Annex IV, regulation 9 of Annex V and regulation 10 of Annex VI;
STCW 1978 - article X;
TONNAGE 1969 - article 12;
AFS 2001 - article 11; and BWM 2004 - article 9.

blocks.p: A.1206(34) revokes A.1185(33), the 2023 Procedures, which had itself followed a long line of revoked predecessors. A great deal of published material still cites A.1185(33) or A.1155(32); at this sitting those are superseded.

A ship flying the flag of a State that is not party to a convention, or a ship below convention size, must not thereby receive more favourable treatment than a ship entitled to fly the flag of a Party. The provisions relied on are SOLAS PROT 1988 article I(3), LL PROT 1988 article I(3), MARPOL article 5(4), STCW article X(5), AFS article 3(3) and BWM article 3(3). Without this rule, non-ratification would be a commercial advantage; with it, the port State applies the convention standard regardless of flag.

blocks.h: 4. How an inspection becomes a detention

blocks.p: The port State control officer begins with certificates and documents and a general impression of the ship's condition. If there are clear grounds for believing that the condition of the ship or its equipment does not correspond substantially with the certificates, or that the crew are not familiar with essential shipboard procedures, the officer proceeds to a more detailed inspection. Deficiencies that are clearly hazardous to safety, health or the environment justify detention: the ship is stopped from proceeding to sea until they are rectified. Detention is reported to the flag State, and the ship may in defined circumstances be permitted to proceed to another port for repair.

blocks.h: 5. The right of appeal - what the instrument actually says

blocks.p: This is the operative provision, and it answers the question directly. Section 2.3.11 of A.1206(34) provides that:

ul: the company or its representative has a right of appeal against a detention taken by the authority of a port State;
the appeal should not cause the detention to be suspended; and
the port State control officer should properly inform the master of the right of appeal.

blocks.p: Three consequences follow, and the question's own framing sets up the first. The right is the company's, not the Chief Engineer's personally. The question asks about "you as the Chief Engineer or the Company", and the instrument answers the disjunction: the Chief Engineer does not hold an independent right of appeal, and acts through, and on behalf of, the company. Second, appealing does not release the ship - the detention runs on while the appeal is heard, so an appeal is never the fastest route back to sea. Third, the officer carries a positive duty to tell the master that the right exists.

blocks.h: 6. What the Chief Engineer should actually do

blocks.p: Because the appeal does not lift the detention, the practical sequence is:

ul: Record the evidence at once - photographs, parameters, alarm and maintenance printouts, the planned maintenance record, the deficiency as written on the report form. Once the ship sails, the evidence is gone.
Ask the officer to identify the convention requirement relied on for each deficiency. A deficiency that cannot be tied to a requirement is the strongest ground of appeal there is.
Notify the company, the flag State and the recognized organization immediately. The flag State may comment on the detention report, and that channel is often more effective than a formal appeal.
Rectify and seek release in parallel. Rectification and release is the mechanism that actually gets the ship to sea.
Let the company lodge the appeal, through the regional MoU's own review mechanism and the port State's administrative or judicial process, supported by the flag State's comments.

blocks.h: 7. Undue delay and compensation, and one trap

blocks.p: Separate from the appeal, the parent conventions require that all possible efforts shall be made to avoid a ship being unduly detained or delayed, and provide that a ship unduly detained or delayed is entitled to compensation for loss or damage suffered - MARPOL article 7(2) and SOLAS regulation I/19. That is a claim for loss, not a mechanism for release, and it is a different remedy from the right of appeal.

The trap. A.1206(34) contains a chapter headed "Review Procedures", and it is not the appeal route. That chapter concerns the Organization's periodic evaluation of summaries of deficiency reports to improve the consistency of port State control worldwide. The owner's remedy is section 2.3.11, inside the general procedural guidelines. The chapter with the right-sounding name is the wrong one.

Eight marks for the concept with focus on the legal framework, and eight for the appeal. The examiner has told you where the marks are in limb (a): a general description of port State control without the conventions behind it answers half the limb. Give the convention list - it is the single most citable thing in the question and very few candidates can produce it. In limb (b), the whole of the credit sits in three propositions: whose right it is, that it does not suspend the detention, and that the master must be told. Everything else is supporting practice.

blocks.h: Whose right is it? The question sets a trap and the instrument springs it

blocks.p: The question asks about "the right to appeal available to you as the Chief Engineer or to the Company". Section 2.3.11 says the right belongs to the company or its representative. The Chief Engineer has no personal right of appeal against a detention; he acts for the company, and the practical value he adds is evidential, not legal. Answering the disjunction explicitly - naming who holds the right and who does not - is exactly what the limb is testing.

blocks.h: An appeal is not a release mechanism

blocks.p: This is the point most answers get wrong, and it is stated in one sentence in the instrument: the appeal should not cause the detention to be suspended. A candidate who writes that the Chief Engineer should appeal in order to get the ship moving has inverted the commercial reality. The ship sails when the deficiencies are rectified and the detention is lifted. The appeal decides whether the detention was right, which matters for the company's record, the ship's risk profile and any claim for loss - but not for tomorrow's sailing.

blocks.h: Port State control does not replace the flag State

blocks.p: The whole architecture rests on the flag State holding primary responsibility, with port State control as a safety net against under-performance. That is why detention is reported to the flag State, why the flag State may comment on the report, and why the flag State route is often the effective one. A ship is not "approved" by passing a port State control inspection; nothing in the Procedures gives an inspection that status.

Saying an appeal suspends or lifts the detention. It does not.

blocks.p:
"The ship is detained. Do you appeal or rectify?" Both, in parallel, and rectification is what returns the ship to service. Saying "appeal" alone shows the candidate does not know the appeal has no suspensive effect.

"The PSCO did not tell the master about any right of appeal. Does that matter?" Yes - 2.3.11 places a duty on the officer to inform the master properly. It is a procedural failure worth recording, and worth raising through the flag State.

"Which chapter of the Procedures gives the owner his remedy?" Section 2.3.11 in the general procedural guidelines - not the chapter titled Review Procedures.

"Your flag State is not party to the BWM Convention. Can the port State inspect ballast water management?" Yes. No more favourable treatment, BWM article 3(3).

blocks.h: 1. The types of loss in marine insurance

blocks.p: Losses divide first into total and partial, and the partial losses divide again. Under the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 the scheme is:

rows: The subject-matter is destroyed, or so damaged that it ceases to be a thing of the kind insured, or the assured is irretrievably deprived of it. A missing ship, after a reasonable time, is presumed an actual total loss.

The subject-matter is reasonably abandoned because actual total loss appears unavoidable, or because it could not be preserved from it without expenditure exceeding its value when saved. Claiming for a constructive total loss requires notice of abandonment.
A partial loss caused accidentally by a peril insured against, which is not a general average loss. It falls solely on the interest damaged - no contribution.
A loss caused by, or directly consequential on, a general average act. It is shared rateably by all the interests saved.
Charges recoverable by a salvor independently of contract, for services rendered in saving the property from peril.

Expenses incurred by or on behalf of the assured for the safety or preservation of the subject-matter, other than general average and salvage charges - the sue and labour expenses. They are not particular average.

blocks.p: The distinction that carries the marks is particular average versus general average: accidental and borne alone, against deliberate and shared.

blocks.h: 2. The general average act, as the York Antwerp Rules 1994 define it

blocks.p: Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules 1994:

"There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure."

Rule A goes on to provide that general average sacrifices and expenditures shall be borne by the different contributing interests on the basis the Rules provide. This wording is unchanged in the 2016 Rules - the later edition merely numbers Rule A's two paragraphs 1 and 2. So the definition asked for is both correct as at 1994 and still correct today, and it is worth saying so rather than leaving the examiner to wonder whether the candidate knows.

blocks.h: 3. When general average may be declared

blocks.p: Every element of Rule A must be present. The absence of any one of them defeats the claim:

ul: there must be a real peril to the common adventure - apprehension alone is not enough;
the act must be extraordinary - not something the ship is already bound to do under the contract of carriage;
it must be intentional and voluntary, not accidental;

it must be reasonable - and the Rule Paramount, which is present in the 1994 Rules, provides that in no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred;
it must be for the common safety of the property in a common maritime adventure, not for one interest alone;
there must be a saving of property - if nothing is saved there is nothing to contribute to.

blocks.p: Typical acts: jettison of cargo, voluntary stranding, water damage from firefighting, machinery damage sustained in refloating, salvage and tug costs, and port-of-refuge expenses. The shipowner declares general average, in practice through the Master; the average adjuster does not declare it, but prepares the adjustment afterwards. Note also that under Rule C, present in the 1994 Rules, there is no allowance in general average for damage to the environment or for loss arising from the escape of pollutant substances.

blocks.h: 4. What the 1994 Rules say that the current Rules do not

blocks.p: The question names a superseded edition deliberately, and the honest answer states the position as at 1994 while identifying the current edition. The York-Antwerp Rules are not law: they are a contractual code, effective only when incorporated into the bill of lading or charterparty, which is why those documents name the edition - and why older contracts incorporating YAR 1994 remain live. YAR 2016 is the current edition. The material differences are:

rows: Expenditure in the nature of salvage is allowed in general average, provided the salvage was for the purpose of preserving the property from peril
Allowed, but subject to exceptions where the parties have separate contractual or legal liability to salvors (the 2004 Rules had made salvage lie where it falls)
A commission of 2 per cent on general average disbursements is allowed (excluding crew wages and maintenance, and fuel and stores not replaced)
No commission; the rule covers only capital loss on goods sold to raise funds, and the cost of insuring disbursements
Fixed at 7 per cent per annum until three months after issue of the adjustment
Rate set annually by reference to a published benchmark: since the technical amendment of October 2022, the USD Prime Rate plus 2 per cent per annum
None. The 1994 Rules end at Rule XXII
Rule XXIII - one year from issue of the adjustment, and in no case more than six years from termination of the adventure

blocks.h: 5. Warranties in marine insurance, and what breach does

blocks.p: A warranty in marine insurance is a promissory warranty - an undertaking by the assured that some thing shall or shall not be done, that some condition shall be fulfilled, or affirming or negativing the existence of a particular state of facts. Two features make it far more severe than a warranty in general contract law:

ul: it must be exactly complied with, whether or not it is material to the risk; and
on breach, the insurer is discharged from liability as from the date of the breach, subject to any express provision in the policy.

blocks.p: Breach is excused only in narrow cases - where a change of circumstances makes the warranty no longer applicable, or where compliance is rendered unlawful by a subsequent law. A jurisdiction point matters here. English law was changed by the Insurance Act 2015, under which breach of warranty now suspends cover rather than discharging the insurer. The Indian position under the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 remains discharge from the date of breach. In an Indian examination, answer on the Indian Act.

blocks.h: 6. Express warranties, with a hull and machinery example

blocks.p: An express warranty is one the parties write into the contract. It must be included in or written upon the policy, or contained in a document incorporated by reference into it. No particular form of words is required - what matters is that the intention to warrant is clear.

Example in a hull and machinery policy: a classification warranty - "warranted that the vessel is classed with a classification society agreed by underwriters and that class is maintained". If class is suspended or withdrawn and the assured does not tell underwriters, the warranty is broken. Equally common are navigation or trading limits - warranting that the vessel will not trade beyond stated geographical limits, or outside stated dates in ice-bound waters - and lay-up warranties requiring the vessel to be laid up in a named port for a stated period.

blocks.h: 7. Implied warranties, and the hull and machinery twist

blocks.p: An implied warranty is imposed by the Act itself and needs no words in the policy. Two matter:

ul: Legality - there is an implied warranty that the adventure insured is a lawful one and that, so far as the assured can control the matter, it shall be carried out in a lawful manner. This warranty cannot be excluded and applies to every marine policy, including hull and machinery.
Seaworthiness - in a voyage policy there is an implied warranty that at the commencement of the voyage the ship shall be seaworthy for the purpose of the particular adventure.

blocks.p: The twist, and it is the discriminator for this limb. A hull and machinery policy is normally a time policy, and in a time policy there is no implied warranty of seaworthiness at any stage of the adventure. But the Act does not leave the point there: where, with the privity of the assured, the ship is sent to sea in an unseaworthy state, the insurer is not liable for any loss attributable to that unseaworthiness. So the correct statement for an H&M policy is that seaworthiness is not warranted, but knowing unseaworthiness defeats the claim on causation - and the best implied-warranty example to give for H&M is therefore legality, which does apply, with the seaworthiness position explained alongside it.

Limb (a) is three tasks in eight marks - a taxonomy, a definition and a list of circumstances - so it must be written economically. The taxonomy is best given as a short table or a tight list; a paragraph of prose on each class will consume the limb before the definition is reached. Limb (b) is two definitions plus two examples, and the examples are worth real marks because the question asks for them expressly "with reference to a hull and machinery policy". An answer that defines express and implied warranties beautifully and gives no H&M example has thrown away half the limb.

blocks.h: The edition question - and the reason it is less dangerous than it looks

blocks.p: The paper names the York Antwerp Rules 1994, an edition superseded twice over. The instinct is to answer on YAR 2016 because it is current. Do not. Answer the question as asked - and then note the current edition. What makes this safe is a fact worth knowing: Rule A is word-for-word identical in 1994 and 2016. The 2016 text only numbers its two paragraphs. So the definition you give is simultaneously the 1994 answer and the modern answer, and saying so demonstrates control of the edition question rather than ignorance of it.

The editions do differ, and the differences are worth two lines: the 1994 Rules allow a 2 per cent commission on disbursements and fix interest at 7 per cent, both of which the modern Rules changed; and the 1994 Rules contain no time bar at all - they end at Rule XXII, and the one-year Rule XXIII first appeared in 2004.

blocks.h: The Rules are contractual, not law

blocks.p: This is the point that explains why the examiner can meaningfully name a 1994 edition in a 2026 paper. The York-Antwerp Rules are not a convention and are not enacted anywhere. They bind only because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them, and the incorporating clause names the edition. A contract written on an older form still applies YAR 1994 today. Absent incorporation, general average falls back on the applicable national law - in India, the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.

blocks.h: Why the warranty limb is harsher than it sounds

blocks.p: In ordinary contract law a "warranty" is the minor term - breach sounds in damages, not termination. In marine insurance it is the opposite: the warranty is the severe term. It must be complied with exactly whether or not it is material to the risk, and breach discharges the insurer from the date of the breach. That inversion is what candidates trip over. Note also that this is where Indian and English law have diverged: the UK Insurance Act 2015 replaced discharge with suspension, so English textbooks now describe a different rule. For an Indian examination, the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 governs.

"The Master jettisons cargo already destroyed by fire. General average?" No. Rule A requires an extraordinary sacrifice of property still of value and at risk; sacrificing what is already lost saves nothing.

blocks.h: 1. Why decarbonisation changes what a marine engineer must be competent at

blocks.p: For a century the marine engineer dealt with one family of fuels whose hazards were broadly the same: a combustible hydrocarbon, hot, oily and familiar. The energy transition replaces that with fuels whose primary hazard is not fire. Ammonia is acutely toxic. Methanol burns with a nearly invisible flame and is toxic by ingestion and absorption. Hydrogen has an extremely wide flammability range and leaks through joints that hold oil. Batteries store energy that cannot be shut off. The competence required is therefore not an incremental extension of existing training - the hazard model itself has changed, and with it the emergency response, the personal protective equipment, the gas detection philosophy and the bunkering procedure.

The driver is regulatory as well as technical. The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships sets the trajectory, and MARPOL Annex VI regulations 25 (EEXI) and 28 (CII) are already in force and already require operational competence in efficiency management and data integrity. At the date of this examination the IMO Net-Zero Framework had been approved but NOT adopted - the extraordinary session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee adjourned in October 2025 without agreement and is due to reconvene later in 2026. The direction is settled; the instrument was not yet in force, and an answer that describes it as adopted is wrong for this sitting.

blocks.h: 2. Where the mandatory training framework reaches - and where it does not

blocks.p: This is the structural point the question rewards. There is presently a gap. Mandatory STCW training exists for gas and low-flashpoint fuels through STCW regulation V/3 and STCW Code section A-V/3, which set basic and advanced training for seafarers serving on ships subject to the IGF Code. But ammonia, methanol, hydrogen and battery-electric propulsion are not yet covered by a mandatory STCW competence standard. Ships are being delivered faster than the Convention can be amended.

IMO has responded with interim guidelines rather than waiting. The Sub-Committee on Human Element, Training and Watchkeeping, meeting in February 2026, four months before this examination, agreed draft interim training guidelines for seafarers on ships using methyl/ethyl alcohol and on ships using ammonia as fuel, prioritised further work on hydrogen fuel cells, LPG, hydrogen, battery-powered ships and wind-assisted propulsion, and carried forward the comprehensive review of the STCW Convention and Code, the long-term route by which these competences will become mandatory. The same session opened a new workstream on fatigue and hours of work and rest.

headers: The concern the training must address
rows: Acute toxicity, not flammability, is the governing hazard. Detection at very low concentrations, respiratory protection and escape sets, water spray and vapour control, medical response to exposure, and bunkering with zero-tolerance leak control. Crews trained to treat a fuel leak as a fire risk will respond to an ammonia leak incorrectly. It is also not a zero-emission fuel: there is no carbon in the molecule, so no direct CO2, but combustion produces N2O - a greenhouse gas far more potent than CO2 - and unburnt ammonia slip, and the lifecycle result depends on how the ammonia was produced. Combustion control and after-treatment therefore become part of the engineer's competence, not just the designer's.

Low flashpoint, an almost invisible flame in daylight, toxicity by ingestion, inhalation and skin absorption, and a much lower energy density requiring larger tanks and altered stability and bunkering planning. Firefighting media differ - alcohol-resistant foam.
Very wide flammability range, very low ignition energy, small-molecule leakage through fittings that would hold oil, material embrittlement, and cryogenic hazards where carried as liquid.

Stored energy that cannot be isolated by closing a valve, thermal runaway and re-ignition, toxic off-gassing, high-voltage isolation, arc-flash protection and permit-to-work discipline for electrical intervention.
Cold burns, brittle fracture of steel, boil-off management, tank rollover, and gas-freeing and inerting procedures.
Deck handling and air-draught management for rotors and sails; high-voltage shore connection procedures and interface responsibility with the terminal.

blocks.h: 4. The competences the transition demands that are not about fuel

ul: Efficiency and data competence. EEXI and CII make the engineer's operating decisions a compliance matter. Hull and propeller condition, trim, speed management and the integrity of the reported data all now carry regulatory consequence, and deliberate or careless misreporting is a serious matter.
Dual-fuel and fuel-flexible operation. Many ships will run on two fuels and change between them at sea, which doubles the failure modes and makes changeover procedure a core competence.

Risk assessment for a novel plant. Where no rule yet exists, the engineer must reason from first principles and from the ship's own risk assessment - which is precisely what an alternative-design approval requires.
Leadership and managerial skill. Introducing an unfamiliar hazard to an experienced crew is a change-management problem before it is a technical one.

blocks.p: The scale of the task is significant: industry research by Lloyd's Register's Maritime Decarbonisation Hub with the Maersk Mc-Kinney Moller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping has estimated that of the order of 800,000 seafarers will require upskilling to handle ammonia safely. That is an industry estimate, not an IMO figure, and should be quoted as such. The Maritime Just Transition Task Force exists to keep seafarers at the centre of that transition rather than at the receiving end of it.

blocks.h: 5. Why communication is a causal factor, not a contributory nicety

blocks.p: Casualty investigation repeatedly finds that the physical failure was survivable and the communication failure was not. A defect known to one watch and not passed to the next, an instruction given but not read back, an assumption that somebody else had closed a valve, a permit issued without the working party understanding its limits - in each case the information existed on board and did not reach the person who needed it. That is why communication is classed as a causal factor: it is not that people communicated badly and an accident coincidentally followed, but that the absence of the information was a link in the causal chain.

Communication failure has recognisable forms: vertical failure, where a junior does not challenge a senior; horizontal failure, between departments - classically engine room and bridge, or ship and terminal; handover failure, at watch or crew change; and ship-to-shore failure, where the vessel's real condition and the office's understanding of it diverge.

ul: ISM Code 1.4.2 makes defined levels of authority and lines of communication between, and amongst, shore and shipboard personnel a functional requirement of the safety management system itself - communication is not an optional good practice, it is something the SMS must provide.

ISM Code 6.6 requires the Company to ensure ship's personnel receive relevant SMS information in a working language or languages understood by them, and 6.7 requires the Company to ensure they can communicate effectively in executing their SMS duties.

SOLAS regulation V/14 requires a working language to be established and recorded in the log-book, with plans and lists translated into it where it is not an official language of the flag State, and requires English on the bridge for bridge-to-bridge, bridge-to-shore and pilot communications unless those involved share another common language.
STCW Code section A-VIII/2 requires watches to be carried out on bridge and engine-room resource management principles, and the management-level competences include leadership and managerial skill.
The IMO Standard Marine Communication Phrases exist to remove ambiguity where a shared natural language cannot be assumed.

blocks.h: 7. Why present-day crewing makes this harder

ul: Multinational, multilingual crews are now the norm rather than the exception. A common working language is a legal requirement but a declared working language is not the same as a shared one, and comprehension under stress falls well below comprehension in conversation.

Reduced manning and high turnover. Short contracts and rotating agency crews mean the informal knowledge that once covered gaps in the written system no longer accumulates. What is not written down is lost at every crew change.

Steep hierarchy and cultural power distance. Where challenging a senior is socially costly, the junior who sees the error says nothing. Resource management training exists precisely to make the challenge legitimate - a closed loop, read back and confirmed, is a technique for defeating rank.

Ship-to-shore intensity. Continuous performance monitoring and remote support mean more decisions are influenced ashore, and the risk is a divergence between the ship's actual condition and the office's picture of it.
Fatigue. Comprehension, assertiveness and read-back discipline all degrade first under fatigue - which is why IMO opened a dedicated workstream on hours of work and rest.

Novel hazards raise the cost of ambiguity. On a conventional ship a misunderstood instruction usually costs time. On an ammonia-fuelled ship, an unclear instruction during bunkering can cost a life - which is the point at which limb (b) rejoins limb (a).

blocks.p: Two limbs of eight, and both use the word "discuss", which means the examiner wants argument rather than a list. Limb (a) expressly asks for examples citing the anticipated areas of concern, so the fuel-by-fuel content is not optional decoration - it is where the marks are. A compact table earns them faster than prose. Limb (b) expressly asks for the present-day shipboard crewing scenarios, so an answer about communication in the abstract, with no reference to multinational crews, short contracts, reduced manning or fatigue, has not answered the question that was set. Ending limb (b) by linking back to the new fuels shows the paper as one argument rather than two.

blocks.h: The gap in the mandatory framework is the strongest single point

blocks.p: Most candidates will write that seafarers need training for new fuels, which is true and unremarkable. The discriminating observation is why the training is not already mandatory: STCW regulation V/3 and Code section A-V/3 cover ships subject to the IGF Code, and ammonia, methanol, hydrogen and batteries fall outside that mandatory competence standard. IMO is bridging the gap with interim guidelines while the comprehensive review of the STCW Convention runs, because ships are arriving faster than the Convention can be amended. That sentence explains the entire state of play.

blocks.h: The temporal anchor - get this right or the answer dates itself

blocks.p: At the date of this paper the IMO Net-Zero Framework was approved but NOT adopted. The extraordinary MEPC session convened in October 2025 adjourned without agreement and was due to reconvene later in 2026, after this examination. A large volume of material published through 2025 asserts that the framework would be adopted and enter into force on a stated timetable; an answer built on that material is wrong for this sitting. Write "approved, not yet adopted" and the point is safe. What is in force, and available to cite without qualification, is MARPOL Annex VI regulations 25 and 28 - EEXI and CII.

The figure of roughly 800,000 seafarers requiring ammonia upskilling comes from industry research by Lloyd's Register's Maritime Decarbonisation Hub with the Maersk Mc-Kinney Moller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping. It is not an IMO figure. Quoting it with its source is stronger than quoting it as though the Organization had published it, and it protects the candidate if challenged on where it comes from.

blocks.h: The hazard model has changed - that is the whole of limb (a)

blocks.p: If a candidate takes one idea from limb (a), it should be that these fuels are not simply "more dangerous oil". A crew drilled to treat a fuel leak as a fire risk will do the wrong thing with ammonia, where the governing hazard is acute toxicity and the correct response is respiratory protection, vapour control and evacuation upwind. Methanol's flame is nearly invisible in daylight. A battery fire cannot be isolated by shutting a valve. Each of those is a training problem precisely because existing instinct is actively wrong, not merely insufficient.

ul: Describing the IMO Net-Zero Framework as adopted or in force. At this sitting it was approved but not adopted.
Claiming there is already mandatory STCW training for ammonia or methanol. There is not; the IGF Code route under STCW V/3 and A-V/3 does not reach them.
Presenting the 800,000 figure as an IMO statistic.
Treating all alternative fuels as one hazard. Toxicity, invisible flame, wide flammability range and stored electrical energy are four different problems.
Writing limb (b) as a general essay on communication with no reference to present-day crewing, which the question expressly asks for.
Citing only 'good communication' as a soft skill, without the instruments - ISM 1.4.2, 6.6 and 6.7, SOLAS V/14 and STCW A-VIII/2 make it a requirement.
Confusing the energy-transition sense of decarbonisation with engine decarbonisation - the maintenance job of removing carbon deposits. They are different subjects that share a word.

blocks.p:
"Ammonia is a fuel. Is your existing fuel-leak drill adequate?" No, and saying so is the point. The existing drill is built around ignition; ammonia's governing hazard is acute toxicity, so detection thresholds, escape sets, water spray, muster position relative to the wind and medical response all differ.

"Which STCW regulation makes alternative-fuel training mandatory?" A trap: none does, for ammonia or methanol. V/3 and A-V/3 cover ships subject to the IGF Code. The gap is being filled by interim guidelines pending the comprehensive STCW review.

"Your crew all speak English. Is the working language requirement satisfied?" Establishing and recording it in the log-book is the requirement, along with translation of posted plans and lists where the working language is not an official language of the flag State. A shared language in practice does not discharge the recorded requirement.

"Why is a read-back required if the order was clear?" Because clarity is judged by the receiver, not the sender, and because a closed loop is what makes a junior's correction socially possible.

questions.understand_first: Both halves of this question are about the same thing: competence the system assumes people have and has not actually taught them. On fuels, the point is not that engineers must work harder at what they already know - it is that the hazard has changed in kind. Heavy fuel oil hurt you by burning. The new fuels hurt you in ways the old training does not reach: one is poisonous well before it is flammable, one burns with a flame you cannot see in daylight, one escapes through joints that would hold oil, and one stores its energy chemically, so you cannot make it safe by shutting a valve. A crew trained for fire is not thereby trained for toxicity. The second half runs on the same logic. Communication is listed as a causal factor rather than a courtesy because almost every shipboard task is a handover, and a handover is only as good as the shared understanding at the join - across languages, across ranks, and among people who may never have sailed together before this contract.

blocks.h: 1. The Code, and the system that implements it

blocks.p: The International Safety Management Code was adopted by resolution A.741(18) on 4 November 1993 and made mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX. Its distinguishing feature is that it prescribes almost no technical requirement. It requires a system, and the system is the Safety Management System. The relationship is precise and worth stating at the outset: the ISM Code states the objectives and the functional requirements; the SMS is the Company's own documented means of meeting them on its ships. Two companies may comply with the same Code with very different systems.

The objectives at paragraph 1.2.1 are to ensure safety at sea, prevention of human injury or loss of life, and avoidance of damage to the environment - in particular to the marine environment - and to property. Paragraph 1.2.2 then requires the Company's safety management objectives to provide for safe practices and a safe working environment, to assess all identified risks to its ships, personnel and the environment and establish appropriate safeguards, and to continuously improve safety management skills of personnel ashore and aboard, including preparation for emergencies.

blocks.h: 2. The components - the functional requirements of an SMS

blocks.p: Paragraph 1.4 sets out what every safety management system must contain:

ul: a safety and environmental protection policy;
instructions and procedures to ensure safe operation of ships and protection of the environment in compliance with relevant international and flag State legislation;
defined levels of authority and lines of communication between, and amongst, shore and shipboard personnel;
procedures for reporting accidents and non-conformities with the provisions of the Code;
procedures to prepare for and respond to emergency situations; and
procedures for internal audits and management reviews.

blocks.p: The Code then expands these across its sections - the safety and environmental protection policy; Company responsibility and authority; the Designated Person ashore with direct access to the highest level of management; the Master's responsibility and overriding authority; resources and personnel; shipboard operations; emergency preparedness; reports and analysis of non-conformities and accidents; maintenance of the ship and equipment, including the identification of critical equipment under 10.3; documentation; and Company verification, review and evaluation.

blocks.h: 3. How the Code is given effect

blocks.p: Compliance is certificated on two levels, and the split matters. The Document of Compliance is issued to the Company, is valid for five years and is subject to annual verification. The Safety Management Certificate is issued to the ship, is valid for five years and is subject to at least one intermediate verification. A ship cannot hold a valid SMC unless its Company holds a valid DOC for that ship type. Certification is the mechanism by which a documented system becomes an enforceable obligation, and it is what a port State control officer will examine first.

blocks.h: 4. Continuous improvement - where it actually lives in the Code

blocks.p: Continuous improvement is not an aspiration attached to the Code; it is written into it in three places and delivered by a closed loop:

ul: 1.2.2.3 requires the Company's objectives to include continuous improvement of safety management skills of personnel ashore and aboard.

Section 9 requires procedures for reporting and analysing non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences, and for implementing corrective action - so failure is required to be surfaced rather than concealed.
Section 12 requires the Company to carry out internal audits, to periodically evaluate the efficiency of the system, and to conduct management review.

blocks.p: The loop runs: policy → procedures → operate → report and analyse → corrective action → audit → management review → revised procedures. Its significance is that it makes the SMS a learning system rather than a filing system. This is also the Code's principal failure mode in practice: a system in which non-conformities are never raised is not a compliant system operating perfectly, it is a broken loop - which is why auditors treat a nil non-conformity return with suspicion rather than approval.

blocks.h: 5. How the Code has evolved - and mostly without amendment

blocks.p: The evolution the question asks about is real, but the mechanism is the interesting part, and it is the observation that lifts this limb. The ISM Code itself has been amended relatively little - the most recent substantive amendments, by resolution MSC.353(92), entered into force on 1 January 2015. Yet the obligations carried by a modern SMS have expanded enormously.

That is possible because the Code was written as a container. Paragraph 1.2.2.2 requires the Company to assess all identified risks - not a listed set of risks - and paragraph 1.4.2 requires procedures ensuring compliance with relevant international and flag State legislation, whatever that legislation becomes. So a new hazard or a new convention obligation enters the SMS without the Code needing to be reopened. The Code has evolved by absorption rather than by amendment.

Cyber risk is the clearest illustration. Resolution MSC.428(98), adopted 16 June 2017, affirms that an approved safety management system should take into account cyber risk management in accordance with the objectives and functional requirements of the ISM Code, and encourages Administrations to ensure that cyber risks are appropriately addressed in safety management systems no later than the first annual verification of the Company's Document of Compliance after 1 January 2021. It did not amend the ISM Code. A cyber risk was simply treated as one of the "all identified risks" paragraph 1.2.2.2 already required to be assessed.

The practical guidance sits in the Guidelines on maritime cyber risk management, MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.3, dated 4 April 2025, which supersedes the earlier revision. Maritime cyber risk is defined there as a measure of the extent to which a Computer Based System is threatened by a potential circumstance or event which may result in shipping-related operational, safety or security failures. The guidance distinguishes information technology from operational technology - the systems that control physical processes - and requires OT to be segmented from IT and protected from internet-facing systems.

The current revision sets out six functional elements, not five. They are Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Govern was added by this revision and requires the risk management strategy and policies to be established and monitored, personnel roles defined, and a person or entity designated as accountable for cyber security with the authority and expertise to discharge it. The elements are expressly not sequential - all should be concurrent and continuous. Much published material still lists five elements, omitting Govern.

Technological advancement presses on the Code in two ways. Increasing automation and integration mean the systems whose sudden operational failure may result in hazardous situations - the critical equipment of section 10.3 - are now as much software and network as they are machinery, and the standby arrangements that section requires to be regularly tested are harder to define for an integrated system. Further ahead, autonomous and remotely operated ships challenge two of the Code's structural assumptions: the Master's overriding authority and the presence of a crew to exercise it. That is a live question for the Organization rather than a settled one.

Environmental sustainability is not new to the Code - avoidance of damage to the environment has been in paragraph 1.2.1 from the beginning, and the required policy is a safety and environmental protection policy. What has changed is the weight of environmental obligation the SMS now carries: garbage and ballast water management, biofouling, and the energy-efficiency regime of MARPOL Annex VI, whose EEXI and CII requirements make operational and data-reporting discipline a compliance matter. Each arrived as procedures under paragraph 1.4.2, without the Code being amended - and the same route will carry the greenhouse gas measures that were approved but not yet adopted at the date of this examination.

Both limbs say "examine", which is stronger than "describe" - the examiner wants analysis, not a recital of the sixteen sections. Limb (a) names three things it wants: role, components and the significance of continuous improvement. The third is where most answers thin out, so give it a section of its own rather than a closing sentence. Limb (b) names three challenges and expects all three to be addressed; an answer that spends the whole limb on cyber has answered one third of it. Sections 1 to 4 are limb (a); 5 to 7 are limb (b).

blocks.h: The strongest argument in limb (b): the Code evolved without being amended

blocks.p: A candidate who lists ISM amendment resolutions is answering a different, duller question. The powerful observation is that the ISM Code has changed remarkably little while the obligations inside a modern SMS have multiplied. That is by design: paragraph 1.2.2.2 requires assessment of all identified risks, and paragraph 1.4.2 requires compliance with relevant legislation - both open-ended. Cyber risk entered the SMS through resolution MSC.428(98) without a single word of the Code being amended. Say that, and the rest of the limb writes itself.

blocks.h: The cyber currency point - six elements, not five

blocks.p: This is the sharpest factual discriminator on the question. The Guidelines were revised to MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.3 on 4 April 2025, approved by MSC 108 and FAL 49. That revision added a sixth functional element, Govern, ahead of Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. An enormous volume of training material, industry guidance and class publication still says five. Writing six, naming Govern, and saying what it requires - accountability, authority and expertise assigned to a named person or entity - is current where almost everything else is not. Note also that the elements are expressly not sequential: they run concurrently and continuously.

blocks.h: Continuous improvement is a loop, and a nil return is a symptom

blocks.p: The mark-winning insight in limb (a) is that continuous improvement is a mechanism, not an attitude: section 9 forces failure to the surface, section 12 audits and reviews, and the corrective action feeds back into the procedures. It follows that a ship reporting no non-conformities is not demonstrating excellence - it is demonstrating that the reporting limb of the loop is not working. Auditors read a nil return as a finding. That single observation shows the candidate understands the Code as a system rather than as a document set.

ul: Listing the sixteen sections of the Code as though that answered "the components of the SMS". The components are the functional requirements at paragraph 1.4; the sections expand them.
Saying the ISM Code was amended to require cyber risk management. It was not - MSC.428(98) applied the existing Code.
Stating five functional elements of cyber risk management. The current revision has six; Govern was added.
Citing MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.2, or the original circular, as current guidance.
Treating environmental protection as a recent addition to the Code. It has been in paragraph 1.2.1 since 1993, and the policy required is a safety and environmental protection policy.
Confusing the Document of Compliance with the Safety Management Certificate, or giving both the same verification regime - the DOC is annual, the SMC has at least one intermediate verification.
Describing the IMO greenhouse gas framework as adopted. At the date of this examination it was approved but not adopted.

blocks.p:
"Your ship has reported no non-conformities in twelve months. Is that good?" No. Section 9 exists to surface them; a nil return usually means the reporting loop has failed, and an auditor will treat it as a finding rather than a commendation.

"Which paragraph of the ISM Code requires cyber risk management?" A trap: none does by name. Paragraph 1.2.2.2 requires assessment of all identified risks, and MSC.428(98) confirms that cyber risk is one of them.

"By when did cyber risk have to be in the SMS?" No later than the first annual verification of the Company's Document of Compliance after 1 January 2021.

"Give me the functional elements of cyber risk management." Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover - six, and not a sequence.

"Who has overriding authority?" The Master, and it is one of the Code's structural assumptions that autonomous operation will have to confront.

ul: Which resolution adopted the ISM Code, and what makes it mandatory? A.741(18); SOLAS chapter IX.
State the functional requirements of an SMS. The six at paragraph 1.4.
Where is continuous improvement required? Paragraph 1.2.2.3, supported by section 9 reporting and analysis and section 12 internal audit and management review.
Who is the Designated Person and what is distinctive about the role? The link ashore with direct access to the highest level of management.
What are the DOC and SMC, and to whom is each issued? DOC to the Company, SMC to the ship; both five years.
Which resolution brought cyber risk into the SMS, and did it amend the Code? MSC.428(98); no.
Which circular carries the cyber guidelines, and what is its current revision? MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3, currently Rev.3 of 4 April 2025.

What does ISM 10.3 require? Identification of equipment and technical systems whose sudden operational failure may result in hazardous situations, with measures to promote reliability including regular testing of standby arrangements.

questions.understand_first: The ISM Code is unusual because it tells you almost nothing about how to run a ship. It tells you to write down how you run your ship, to do what you wrote, to record it when you did not, and to change what you wrote when the record shows it was wrong. Everything else - cyber, emissions, new fuels - gets carried inside that same loop without the Code itself having to change.

blocks.h: 1. The three cost families, and what actually distinguishes them

blocks.p: The three are separated by what makes the money go out, not by size. That test is what allows the Chief Engineer to see where he has leverage:

rows: Fixed. Incurred whether the ship trades, waits or lies idle.
Keeping the ship in a state fit to trade
Largely fixed in the short run. Incurred whether or not the ship is on a voyage.
Variable. Incurred only when, and because, the ship sails.

ul: Capital costs - the newbuilding or purchase price, debt service and interest, depreciation, and the return required on the owner's equity. Major capital expenditure such as a retrofit or a conversion also falls here rather than in maintenance.

Operating costs - crew wages, victualling and travel; stores and consumables including lubricating oil and chemicals; spares; repairs and maintenance; insurance, both hull and machinery and protection and indemnity; registration and flag State fees; classification fees; and shore management and administration. Periodic maintenance - drydocking and special survey - is often separated out because it is lumpy rather than continuous.

Voyage costs - bunker fuel, which normally dominates; port dues and charges; canal transit dues; pilotage and towage. Cargo-handling costs are sometimes treated as a fourth family, since whether they fall on owner or charterer depends on the charterparty.

blocks.h: 3. The Chief Engineer's leverage - and where he has none

blocks.p: Being honest about this is what separates a management answer from a list:

ul: Capital cost - effectively no short-run influence. The price was paid and the loan was signed before the Chief Engineer joined. His influence is indirect and long-run: a ship maintained to a good standard with complete, credible records commands a better residual value and a cleaner class record, and a well-argued technical business case is what gets a retrofit approved or rejected.
Voyage cost - the largest single lever he holds, because fuel is the dominant voyage cost and fuel consumption is a function of machinery and hull condition and of how the plant is operated.
Operating cost - shared with the office. Crew cost, insurance and flag fees are set ashore. Maintenance, spares, stores, lubricating oil and the drydock specification are substantially his.

Hull and propeller condition. Fouling raises the power required for a given speed and is often the largest single recoverable loss on a ship. Systematic performance monitoring - power and consumption against speed, corrected for draught, trim, wind and sea - is what turns "the ship feels slow" into a costed case for a hull clean or propeller polish.

Machinery condition and performance. Indicator and pressure-rise data, turbocharger condition, air and gas differential pressures, cooler and economiser fouling, and correct injection condition all show up directly in specific fuel consumption.

Correct operation for the loading in use. Slow steaming saves fuel but pushes the engine into a region it was not optimised for; running it there without the correct measures raises maintenance cost and can cost more than the fuel saved.

Fuel management. Bunker quantity survey and sampling at delivery, correct treatment and settling, avoiding commingling of incompatible fuels, and minimising sludge - a fuel dispute or an off-specification bunker can erase a year of careful savings.
Auxiliary and hotel load. Generator loading, boiler and steam management, shaft generator use where fitted, and in-port load reduction.

The regulatory overlay. Under MARPOL Annex VI regulations 25 and 28, the EEXI and CII requirements make efficiency a compliance outcome, not merely a cost. The same engineering decisions now carry a rating consequence and a data-integrity obligation.

Maintenance strategy. Breakdown maintenance is the most expensive way to run machinery; time-based maintenance overhauls items that were still serviceable; condition-based maintenance spends the money when the evidence says it is needed. The Chief Engineer's real contribution is choosing the right strategy for each item rather than applying one to all.
Off-hire avoidance. A day off-hire usually costs more than the repair that caused it. Ranking maintenance by the consequence of failure, rather than by convenience, is the discipline.
Lubricating oil management. Feed-rate optimisation, correct base number for the fuel in use, and onboard and laboratory analysis to catch wear early.

Drydock specification. The docking is the single largest operating-cost event the Chief Engineer materially controls. A specification written from real condition data, with growth work anticipated, prevents the change orders that make dockings overrun.
Spares and stores control - which is the third part of the question.

blocks.h: 6. Modern principles of inventory control - classifying the stock

blocks.p: Modern inventory control begins by recognising that not all items deserve the same control. The techniques are ways of deciding which item gets which treatment:

rows: A small proportion of items carries most of the value. Concentrate ordering effort, accuracy and review on A items; control C items loosely and in bulk.
Criticality of the consequence of not having it
Vital, Essential, Desirable. The marine-critical technique, because a cheap item can be vital.
Fast, Slow, Non-moving. Exposes dead stock and obsolete holdings.
Scarce, Difficult, Easy. Drives lead time and safety stock.
Governs custody, security and authorisation levels.

blocks.p: The important move is to combine them. ABC alone will under-protect a cheap but vital item; VED alone will over-protect an expensive but non-critical one. The practical shipboard method is the ABC-VED matrix: value on one axis, criticality on the other, with the highest control applied to anything Vital regardless of value. This is where the regulatory constraint enters: ISM Code paragraph 10.3 requires the Company to identify equipment whose sudden operational failure may result in hazardous situations and to provide measures promoting its reliability. That identified list and the V of a VED classification should be the same list.

blocks.h: 7. Modern principles - ordering, and the limits of just-in-time at sea

ul: Economic order quantity balances the cost of ordering against the cost of holding, giving the order size at which their sum is least. It is a useful idea afloat and an unreliable formula, because the "ordering cost" for a moving asset is dominated by logistics to a port the ship has not reached yet.

Reorder level and minimum-maximum. Reorder level is average consumption over the lead time plus a safety stock. On a ship the lead time is the hard variable - it is not the supplier's despatch time but the time until the ship is somewhere the part can reach it.
Safety stock buffers variability in both demand and lead time, and should be set by criticality rather than uniformly.
Lead-time and voyage-plan integration. Ordering is planned against the trading pattern, so that deliveries fall where the ship will actually be and agency and freight costs are contained.

Standardisation and fleet pooling. Common makers and models across a fleet cut the number of distinct items held, allow stock to be shared between ships and pooled at a hub port, and improve buying power.
Vendor-managed inventory and framework agreements with makers and service providers, which move some holding cost and obsolescence risk onto the supplier.

Computerised inventory integrated with the planned maintenance system, so that consumption is booked against the job that used it and future demand becomes predictable rather than anecdotal. Condition-based maintenance strengthens this further: the better the prediction of when an item will be needed, the less stock is required to achieve the same availability.

Obsolescence and shelf-life control. Rubber, gaskets, batteries and chemicals expire on the shelf; first-in-first-out issue and a periodic dead-stock review under FSN prevent a store full of unusable items.

blocks.p: Just-in-time deserves a qualification rather than a recommendation. Minimising holding is sound for consumables and for non-critical, easily obtained items. It is not appropriate for critical spares, because a ship is a moving asset whose supply lead time is uncertain, and because the consequence of a stockout is not a delayed production line but a hazardous situation of exactly the kind ISM 10.3 requires to be guarded against. The correct modern position is just-in-time where the consequence of being wrong is commercial, and safety stock where it is not.

Sixteen marks, no printed limbs, but three unmistakable tasks: the cost families, the Chief Engineer's role, and inventory control. Treat them as roughly a third each and none can be forgotten - the commonest failure on this question is a long, confident description of shipping costs followed by three lines on inventory, discarding a third of the marks. The examiner has put "What are the modern management principles used in Inventory control?" as a separate sentence precisely because it is a separate block of credit.

blocks.h: Define the families by their trigger, not by examples

blocks.p: Weak answers list items under three headings and hope the classification is self-evident. Strong answers state the test first: capital cost is triggered by owning the ship, operating cost by keeping it fit to trade, and voyage cost by performing a particular voyage. Once that is on the page, every borderline item can be placed and defended - and it explains why the same expense can move between families, which is exactly what an examiner will probe.

blocks.h: Be honest about where the Chief Engineer has no influence

blocks.p: This is a management question, and management judgement includes knowing what you do not control. A candidate who claims to optimise capital cost is not credible: the price was paid and the finance arranged before he joined. The strong answer says so, and then makes the two real long-run points - that maintained condition and complete records protect residual value, and that the technical business case is what gets capital expenditure approved. Conceding the point costs nothing and buys authority for the rest of the answer.

blocks.h: This question rests on practice, not on regulation - and that is not a weakness

blocks.p: There is no IMO instrument on ship cost structure and none on inventory control. The correct response is not to decorate the answer with SOLAS, MARPOL or ISM references that do not bear on the point. Reach for regulation only where it genuinely applies, and there are exactly two places: ISM Code 10.3, which makes critical-equipment identification a requirement and therefore constrains spares policy; and MARPOL Annex VI regulations 25 and 28, which turn fuel efficiency into a compliance outcome. Two well-placed citations in an otherwise engineering-and-management answer read as competence. Six irrelevant ones read as padding.

blocks.h: VED matters more than ABC at sea, and ABC-VED matters more than either

blocks.p: ABC analysis is the technique everyone remembers, and on a ship it is the less useful of the two. ABC ranks by value; a ship is stopped by a cheap item as easily as by an expensive one. VED ranks by the consequence of not having it, which is the question that actually matters afloat. The mark-winning statement is that the two are combined - highest control to anything Vital regardless of value - and that the Vital list should be the same list the Company already has to identify under ISM 10.3. That single sentence connects a management technique to a regulatory obligation correctly, which is rare.

ul: Answering only the cost half and leaving inventory control to a closing paragraph.
Putting bunkers in operating cost. Fuel burned on a voyage is a voyage cost.
Putting drydocking in capital cost. It is maintenance - normally treated within operating cost, often shown separately as periodic maintenance. A conversion or retrofit is capital.
Claiming to reduce capital cost from the engine room.
Recommending just-in-time for critical spares without qualification.
Explaining ABC analysis and stopping, without VED - and so never reaching criticality.
Quoting specific percentage shares of cost as though they were universal. They vary by ship type, trade, flag and market.
Attaching SOLAS, STCW or ISM references to management techniques they have nothing to do with.

blocks.p:
"Would you run just-in-time on this ship?" For consumables and easily obtained non-critical items, yes. For critical spares, no - the lead time to a moving ship is uncertain and the consequence of a stockout is a hazardous situation, not a production delay. The qualification is the answer.

"Your A-class item and your V-class item are different items. Which gets the tighter control?" The V item. Value tells you what the stock is worth; criticality tells you what its absence costs.

"You have saved a great deal of fuel by slow steaming. Have you saved money?" Not necessarily. Sustained low-load operation outside the range the engine was optimised for raises maintenance cost, and the net position has to be argued, not assumed.

"Which cost family does the Chief Engineer influence most?" Voyage cost, through fuel - and it is worth saying that this is also the one now carrying a regulatory consequence under EEXI and CII.

ul: Name the three cost families and the test that separates them. Owning, keeping fit to trade, performing a voyage.
Which is the largest voyage cost? Bunker fuel, normally by a wide margin.
Where does insurance sit? Operating cost. Where do canal dues sit? Voyage cost.
Distinguish ABC from VED. Value against criticality.
What is the reorder level? Average consumption over the lead time, plus safety stock.
What does FSN expose? Non-moving and obsolete stock.
Which ISM paragraph makes critical-equipment identification a requirement? 10.3.
Why is EOQ unreliable on a ship? Because ordering cost is dominated by logistics to a moving asset, not by the paperwork of placing the order.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of authority for this question

blocks.p: This is the question on the paper with the thinnest regulatory foundation, and the answer says so rather than disguising it. The cost taxonomy and every inventory-control technique named here are accepted management and shipping-economics practice, not the content of any IMO, statutory or class instrument. They are presented as reasoning and practice, and no attempt has been made to give them an authority they do not have - which is a deliberate decision, because attaching irrelevant convention references to a management technique is a worse error than admitting that none applies. Two constraints genuinely do apply and are used only where they bite: ISM 10.3 and MARPOL Annex VI regulations 25 and 28. No numerical cost proportions are quoted - the share of operating cost taken by crew, or of voyage cost by bunkers - because they vary by ship type, trade, flag and market and MIW holds no verified dataset. Any figure a candidate has seen quoted should be treated as illustrative of one segment at one time. Finally, no claim is made that any flag Administration or classification society mandates a specific minimum spare-gear scale, because that was not established.

questions.understand_first: The three cost families are not three sizes of bill - they are three different triggers, and that distinction is what earns the marks. One is incurred by owning the ship at all, whether or not she ever moves. One is incurred by keeping her fit to trade - crewed, stored, maintained, insured - and it carries on while she sits in port. One is incurred only because a particular voyage is being performed, and it stops when the voyage stops. Test any item by asking what makes it arise, and bunkers land where candidates least expect them. That framework then tells you immediately where a Chief Engineer has leverage and where he has none. He cannot alter what the ship cost to buy. He can move fuel consumption substantially - through hull and machinery condition, loading, and how the plant is run - and that is the largest single number he touches. Inventory follows the same discipline: not every item on board deserves equal attention, so you classify before you order.
